label: Lemma 1.1
content:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a field and $P$ be an irreducible polynomial over $\Bbbk$. For $Q\in\Bbbk[X]$, we have :
$P(X+Q(X))=P(X)+P^{\prime}(X)Q(X)+R(X)Q(X)^{2},$
for some $R\in\Bbbk[X]$.
proof:
Set $P(X)=\sum a_{i}X^{i}$. We get
$P(X+Q(X))=\sum a_{i}(X+Q(X))^{i}=\sum a_{i}(X^{i}+iX^{i-1}Q(X)+R_{i}(X)Q(X)^{2}),$
for some $R_{i}\in\Bbbk[X]$. But $\sum_{i>0}ia_{i}x^{i-1}=P^{\prime}(X)$ and $\sum a_{i}X^{i}=P(X)$. This proves the proposition. ∎

label: Lemma 1.2
content: Let $\Bbbk$ be a field and $P$ be an irreducible polynomial over $\Bbbk$. If $P^{\prime}\neq 0$, then we have an infinite sequence of pairs of polynomials $(Q_{0},R_{0}),(Q_{1},R_{1}),\cdots$ such that for $k\geq 0$ we have : $P(X+\sum_{i=1}^{k}Q_{i}(X)P(X)^{i})=R_{k}(X)P(X)^{k+1}.$
proof:
For $k=0$, the equation is $P(X)=R_{0}(X)P(X)$. We can take any $Q_{0}$ and we take $R_{0}(X)=1$. We will prove the propostion by induction. Assume that the pairs $(Q_{0},R_{0}),\cdots,(Q_{n},R_{n})$ are constructed, we will constuct $(Q_{n+1},R_{n+1})$. Applying the previous lemma we get that for $U$ and $S$ in $\Bbbk[X]$, we have:

$P(U(X)+S(X)P(X)^{n+1})=P(U(X))+P^{\prime}(U(X))S(X)P(X)^{n+1}+T(X)P(X)^{2n+2}.$

For $U(X)=X+\sum_{i=1}^{n}Q_{i}(X)P(X)^{i}$ the eqution is reduced by the induction hypothesis to :

$P(U(X)+S(X)P(X)^{n+1})=(R_{n}(X)+P^{\prime}(U(X))S(X))P(X)^{n+1}+T(X)P(X)^{2n+2},$

and we get a pair $(Q_{n+1},S_{n+1})$ if we find $S(X)$ such that $R_{n}(X)+P^{\prime}(U(X))S(X)$ is zero modulo $P(X)$ (i.e. a multiple of $P(X)$). But $P$ is irreducible. Hence $\Bbbk[X]/(P)$ is a field and the class of $P^{\prime}\circ U$ in this field is equal to the class of $P^{\prime}$ wich is invertible since $P^{\prime}\neq 0$. So $P^{\prime}\circ U$ is invertible modulo $P$ and therefore we can find an $S(X)$ such that $R_{n}(X)+P^{\prime}(U(X))S(X)$ is zero modulo $P$. This proves the proposition. ∎

label: Proposition 1.3
content: Let $\Bbbk$ be a field and $P$ be an irreducible polynomial over $\Bbbk$. If $P^{\prime}\neq 0$, then we have an injective $\Bbbk$-algebra morphism from the field $\Bbbk[X]/(P)$ into $\Bbbk[X]/(P^{k})$, for $k\geq 1$.
proof:
Let $Q_{0},Q_{1},\cdots,Q_{k-1}$ be as in the previous proposition and let $\phi_{k}:\Bbbk[X]\to\Bbbk[X]/(P^{k})$ be the $\Bbbk$-algebra morphism given by

$X\mapsto X+\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}Q_{i}(X)P(X)^{i}.$

By the previous proposition $\phi_{k}$ maps $P$ to $0$ and hence induces an algebra morphism $\bar{\phi}_{k}:\Bbbk[X]/(P)\to\Bbbk[X]/(P^{k})$. To see that $\bar{\phi}_{k}$ is injective, notice that $\pi_{k}\circ\bar{\phi}_{k}(X)=X$, where $\pi_{k}$ is the projection $\Bbbk[X]/(P^{k})\mapsto\Bbbk[X]/(P),\ X\mapsto X$.

label: Corollary 1.4
content: Let $\Bbbk$ be a field and $P$ be an irreducible polynomial over $\Bbbk$. If $P^{\prime}\neq 0$, then the local ring $\Bbbk[X]/(P^{k})$ contains its residue field $\Bbbk[X]/(P)$ as a $\Bbbk$-subalgebra.

label: Corollary 1.5
content: Let $\Bbbk$ be a field and $P$ be an irreducible polynomial over $\Bbbk$. If $P^{\prime}\neq 0$, then the local ring $\Bbbk[X]/(P^{k})$ is a $\Bbbk[X]/(P)$-algebra.

label: Lemma 1.6
content: Let $\Bbbk$ be a field and $P$ be an irreducible polynomial over $\Bbbk$. If $P^{\prime}\neq 0$, then the family $1,P,P^{2},\cdots,P^{k-1}$ of $K[X]/(P^{k})$ is free over $\Bbbk[X]/(P)$.
proof: Assume that $a_{0}1+a_{1}P+\cdots a_{k-1}P^{k-1}=0$ for given $a_{i}\in\Bbbk[X]/(P)$. We want to prove that $a_{0}=\cdots=a_{k-1}=0$. To see that multiply the equation $P^{k-1}$, we get $a_{0}P^{k-1}=0..$ Hence $a_{0}=0$. Since $a_{0}=0$, multuplying the first equation of the proof by $P^{k-2}$, we get that $a_{1}P^{k-1}=0$ and hence as before we deduce that $a_{1}=0$. We show that $a_{i}=0$ for all the remaining $i$’s by multiplying successively by $P^{k-3},P^{k-4},\dots$.

label: Theorem 1.7
content: Let $\Bbbk$ be a field and $P$ be an irreducible polynomial over $\Bbbk$. If $P^{\prime}\neq 0$, then $\Bbbk[X]/(P^{k})$ is isomorphic as a $\Bbbk[X]/(P)$-algebra and as a $\Bbbk$-algebra to $(\Bbbk[X]/(P))[Y]/(Y^{k}).$ The isomorphism is given by $Y\mapsto P$.
proof: One has a unique $\Bbbk[X]/(P)$-algebra morphism $\psi_{k}:(\Bbbk[X]/(P))[Y]/(Y^{k})\to\Bbbk[X]/(P^{k})$ given by $Y\mapsto P$. This morphism is injective by the previous lemma. The morphism $\psi_{k}$, is also a $\Bbbk$-algebra morphism. The dimension of $\Bbbk[X]/(P^{k})$ over $\Bbbk$ is equal to the degree of $P^{k}$, hence equal to $k\cdot deg(P)$ ($deg(P)$ is the degree of $P$). The algebra $(\Bbbk[X]/(P))[Y]/(Y^{k})$ is also of dimension $k\cdot deg(P)$ over $\Bbbk$. We therefore have that $\psi_{k}$ is an injective $\Bbbk$-linear map between two vector spaces having the same dimension over $\Bbbk$. This proves that $\psi_{k}$ is an isomorphism. ∎

label: Theorem 1.8
content: Let $\Bbbk$ be a field. Let $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ be two irreducible polynomials over $\Bbbk$ and $k$ a positive integer. If $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are separable (i.e. $P^{\prime}_{i} \neq 0$), then the local rings $\Bbbk[X]/(P^{k}_{1})$ and $\Bbbk[X]/(P^{k}_{2})$ are isomorphic if and only if their residue fields $\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1})$ and $\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2})$ are isomorphic.
proof: If the local rings are isomorphic, then the residue fields are isomorphic. Since we assume that $P_i' \neq 0$, by the previous theorem we have that $\Bbbk[X]/(P_i^k)$ is isomorphic to $(\Bbbk[X]/(P_i))[Y]/(Y^n)$. The "only if" part of the statement follows. ∎

label: Proposition 1.10
content: Let $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ be two irreducible polynomials over $\Bbbk$ and $k$ a positive integer. If $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are seprable ($i.e.$ $P^{\prime}_{i}\neq 0$), then the local rings $\Bbbk[X]/(P^{k}_{1})$ and $\Bbbk[X]/(P^{k}_{2})$ are isomorphic as $\Bbbk$-algebras if and only if their residue fileds $\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1})$ and $\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2})$ are isomorphic as $\Bbbk$-algebras.
proof: The proof of the previous theorem can be adapted to obtain the proposition. ∎

label: Definition 2.1
content: For $A$ and $B$ two $\Bbbk$-algebras, we say that a ring morphism $f:A\to B$ stabilizes $\Bbbk$ if there exists a field automorphism $\sigma_f:\Bbbk\to\Bbbk$ such that $f(a)=\sigma_f(a)$ for all $a\in\Bbbk$.

label: Proposition 2.2
content:
$\Bbbk$ is a field. Let $A$ and $B$ be two finite dimensional algebras over $\Bbbk$ and $f:A\to B$ be a ring morphism stabilizing $\Bbbk$.

1. $Im(f)$ is a vector subspace of $B$.
2. If $f$ is injective then $dim(Im(f))=dim(A)$.
3. If $f$ is injective and $dim(A)=dim(B)$ then $f$ is an isomorphism.
4. If $f$ is an isomorphism then $f^{-1}$ stabilizes $\Bbbk$ and $\sigma_{f^{-1}}=\sigma_{f}^{-1}$.
5. If $f$ is an isomorphism then $dim(A)=dim(B)$.
6. Let $I$ be a proper ideal of $B$, and let $\pi:B\mapsto B/I$ be the projection. The ring morphism $\pi\circ f$ stabilizes $\Bbbk$ and $\sigma_{\pi\circ f}=\sigma_{f}$.
7. Let $J$ be an ideal of $A$ lying in the kernel of $f$. The morphism $\bar{f}:A/J\to B$ factorising $f$ stabilizes $\Bbbk$ and $\sigma_{\bar{f}}=\sigma_{f}$.
proof: This can be proved as for $\Bbbk$-algebra morphisms, we only need to use $\sigma_{f}$ and $\sigma_{f}^{-1}$. ∎

label: Proposition 2.3
content: $\Bbbk$ is a field. Let $\sigma:\Bbbk\to\Bbbk$ be a field automorphism. We have a unique well defined ring automorphism $\sigma^{X}:\Bbbk[X]\to\Bbbk[X]$ stabilizing $\Bbbk$ given by the data $\sigma^{X}(X)=X$ and $\sigma_{\sigma^{X}}=\sigma$.

label: Proposition 2.4
content:
$\Bbbk$ is a field and $P_{1},P_{2}$ are irreducible polynomials in $\Bbbk[X]$. If $f:\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1})\to\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2})$ is a ring isomorphism stabilizing $\Bbbk$ then :

1. The degree of $P_{1}$ is equal to the degree of $P_{2}$.
2. There exist a unique polynomial $Q_{f}\in\Bbbk[X]$ of degree less than the degree of $P_{1}$ (the degree of $P_{2}$) and greater or equal to $1$ such that $f$ is induced by the ring morphism stabilizing $\Bbbk$ $f_{X}:\Bbbk[X]\to\Bbbk[X]$ defined by $X\mapsto Q_{f}$ and $\sigma_{f_{X}}=\sigma_{f}$ i.e. $P\mapsto\sigma_{f}^{X}(P)\circ Q_{f}$, where $\sigma_{f}^{X}$ is as in the previous proposition.
3. $\sigma_{f}^{X}(P_{1})\circ Q_{f}=S_{f}P_{2}$ for a given $S_{f}\in\Bbbk[X]$.
4. For $P\in K[X]$, if $\sigma_{f}^{X}(P)\circ Q_{f}=SP_{2}$ for some $S\in\Bbbk[X]$ then $P=RP_{1}$ for some $R\in\Bbbk[X]$.
5. The morphism $f_{X}$ maps $(P_{1}^{n})$ into $(P_{2}^{n})$ and hence induces a ring morphism stabilizing $\Bbbk$ : $f_{X,n}:\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1}^{n})\to\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2}^{n})$ induced by $P\mapsto\sigma_{f}^{X}(P)\circ Q_{f}$.
proof: Point 1) follows from the fact that the dimension of $\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1})$ and $\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2})$ as $\Bbbk$-vector spaces are respectively the degree of $P_{1}$ and the degree of $P_{2}$. Now, there is a unique polynomial $Q_{f}$ of $\Bbbk[X]$ of degree less than the degree of $P_{2}$ (degree of $P_{1}$) such that $f(X_{1})=Q_{f}(X_{2})$ where $X_{1}$ is the class of $X$ in $\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1})$ and $X_{2}$ is the class of $X$ in $\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2})$. This polynomial has a degree greater or equal to $1$ otherwise the image of $f$ will lie in $\Bbbk$ ($f$ stabilizes $\Bbbk$). For $P\in K[X]$ we have $f(P(X_{1}))=\sigma_{f}^{X}(P)\circ Q_{f}(X_{2})$. This proves 2). Since $P_{1}(X_{1})=0$, $f(P_{1}(X_{1}))=\sigma_{f}^{X}(P)\circ Q_{f}(X_{2})=0$. Hence, $\sigma_{f}^{X}(P)\circ Q_{f}$ lies in the ideal $(P_{2})$. This proves 3). The statement in 4) is equivalent to the injectivity of $f$. Finally 3) imples that $\sigma_{f}^{X}(P_{1}^{n})\circ Q_{f}=S_{f}^{n}P_{2}^{n}$. This proves 5). We have proved the proposition. ∎

label: Proposition 2.5
content: $\Bbbk$ is a field and $P_{1},P_{2}$ are irreducible polynomials in $\Bbbk[X]$. Let $f:\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1})\to\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2})$ be a ring isomorphism stabilizing $\Bbbk$ and let $S_{f}$ and $f_{X,n}$ be as in the previous proposition. For $n>1$, $S_{f}$ is prime to $P_{2}$ if and only if $f_{X,n}:\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1}^{n})\to\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2}^{n})$ is an isomorphism.
proof:
We first prove that if $S_{f}$ is prime to $P_{2}$ then the map $f_{X,n}$ is an isomorphism. Assume that $S_{f}$ is prime to $P_{2}$ and take $P\in K[X]$ such that its class $\bar{P}$ in $\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1}^{n})$ lies in the

### Page 5
kernel of $f_{X,n}$, i.e. $\sigma_f^X (P)\circ Q_f = SP_2^n$ for some $S\in K[X]$ ($Q_{f}$ of the previous proposition). Let $m$ be the largest integer for wich $P_1^m$ divides $P$. We have $P = TP_1^m$ for some $T\in \mathbb{k}[X]$. Combining the last two equation and by applying 3) of the previous proposition we get :

$$\sigma_ {f} ^ {X} (P) \circ Q _ {f} = \sigma_ {f} ^ {X} (T P _ {1} ^ {m}) \circ Q _ {f} = (\sigma_ {f} ^ {X} (T) \circ Q _ {f}) S _ {f} ^ {m} P _ {2} ^ {m} = S P _ {2} ^ {n}.$$

Assume $m < n$. Since we assumed that $S_{f}$ is prime to $P_{2}$, we get that $\sigma_{f}^{X}(T) \circ Q_{f} = S' P_{2}^{n - m}$ with $n - m \geq 1$ and hence by 4) of the previous proposition $T = RP_{1}$ for some $R \in \mathbb{k}[X]$. Since $P = TP_{1}^{m}$, we now have $P = R_{1}P_{1}^{m + 1}$. This leads to a contradiction, since $m$ is the largest integer for wich $P_{1}^{m}$ divides $P$. Therefore the assumption $m < n$ is false and $P = TP_{1}^{m}$ with $m \geq n$. This proves that $P \in (P_{1}^{n})$ and the class $\bar{P}$ of $P$ in $\mathbb{k}[X] / (P_1^n)$ is 0. We have proved that if $S_{f}$ is prime to $P$ then $f_{X,n}$ is injective. Since, $\mathbb{k}[X] / (P_1^n)$ and $\mathbb{k}[X] / (P_2^n)$ have the same dimensions as vector spaces over $\mathbb{k}$ (follows from 1) of the previous proposition). We deduce that if $S_{f}$ is prime to $P$ then the morphism $f_{X,n}$ is an isomorphism. Let us prove the converse. For that assume that $S_{f}$ is not prime to $P_{2}$. Hence, (by 3) of the previous proposition) and the fact that $P_{2}$ is irreducible, we have :

$$\sigma_ {f} ^ {X} (P _ {1}) \circ Q _ {f} = S P _ {2} ^ {m},$$

for some $m > 1$ and some $S \in \mathbb{k}[X]$. If $n = 2$, we see from the equation that the (nonzero) class of $P_{1}$ in $\mathbb{k}[X] / (P_1^2)$ lies in the kernel of $f_{X,n}$. For $n > 2$, denote by $q_{n,m}$ the quotient of the division of $n$ by $m$. We have $(q_{n,m} + 1)m \geq n$ and $q_{n,m} + 1 < n$. With these conditions, we remark by raising the last equation to the power $q_{n,m} + 1$ that the nonzero class of $P_1^{q_{n,m} + 1}$ in $\mathbb{k}[X] / (P_1^n)$ lies in the kernel of $f_{X,n}$. We have proved that if $S_f$ is not prime to $P_2$ then the morphism $f_{X,n}$ is not an isomorphism.

For $f: \mathbb{k}[X] / (P_1) \to \mathbb{k}[X] / (P_2)$ a ring isomorphisms stabilizing $\mathbb{k}$, we will use $Q_f$ and $S_f$ and $\sigma_f^X$ without refrencing.

label: Proposition 2.6
content:
$\Bbbk$ is a field and $P_{1},P_{2}$ are irreducible polynomials in $\Bbbk[X]$. Let $f: \mathbb{k}[X] / (P_1) \to \mathbb{k}[X] / (P_2)$ be a ring isomorphism stabilizing $\mathbb{k}$.

1) If $\alpha$ is a root of $P_{2}$ then $Q_{f}(\alpha)$ is a root of $\sigma_f^X (P_1)$.
2) We have a bijection $\{\text{roots of } P_2\} \to \{\text{roots of } \sigma_f^X(P_1)\}$ given by $\alpha \mapsto Q_f(\alpha)$.
proof:
1) follows from the equation $\sigma_f^X(P_1) \circ Q = S_f P_2$ of proposition 2.4 and it follows from 1) that we have a map $g: \{\text{roots of } P_2\} \to \{\text{roots of } \sigma_f^X(P_1)\}$ given by $\alpha \mapsto Q_f(\alpha)$. To prove 2) we will define an inverse to $g$. Applying 3) of proposition 2.4 to $f^{-1}$ we get that:

$$
(\sigma_ {f} ^ {X}) ^ {- 1} (P _ {2}) \circ Q _ {f ^ {- 1}} = S _ {f ^ {- 1}} P _ {1},
$$

and hence

$$
P _ {2} \circ \sigma_ {f} ^ {X} (Q _ {f ^ {- 1}}) = \sigma_ {f} ^ {X} (S _ {f ^ {- 1}}) \sigma_ {f} ^ {X} (P _ {1}).
$$

Therefore we have a well defined map $h: \{\text{roots of } \sigma_f^X(P_1)\} \to \{\text{roots of } P_2\}$ given by $\alpha \mapsto \sigma_f^X(Q_{f^{-1}})(\alpha)$. We will prove that $h$ and $g$ are inverse to each other. Since $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are inverse to each other, we have:

$$
\sigma_ {f} ^ {X} (Q _ {f ^ {- 1}}) \circ Q _ {f} = X + S _ {2} P _ {2} \quad \text{and} \quad (\sigma_ {f} ^ {X}) ^ {- 1} (Q _ {f}) \circ Q _ {f ^ {- 1}} = X + S _ {1} P _ {1},
$$

for some $S_1, S_2 \in \mathbb{k}[X]$. The first equation shows that $hg$ is the identity of $\{\text{roots of } P_2\}$. Composing the second equation by $\sigma_f^X$ we obtain that $gh$ is the identity of $\{\text{roots of } \sigma_f^X(P_1)\}$. We have proved 2).

label: Proposition 2.7
content: $\Bbbk$ is a field and $P_{1},P_{2}$ are irreducible polynomials in $\Bbbk[X]$. Let $f:\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1})\to\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2})$ be a ring isomorphism stabilizing $\Bbbk$. $S_{f}$ is prime to $P_{2}$ If and only if $Q^{\prime}_{f}\neq 0$.
proof:
We first note that $\sigma^{X}_{f}(P_{1})$ is irreducible since $P_{1}$ is irreducible and $\sigma^{X}_{f}$ is an automorphism of $\Bbbk[X]$. Since that $\sigma^{X}_{f}(P_{1})$ and $P_{2}$ have the same degree ( 1) of proposition 2.4), that $\sigma^{X}_{f}(P_{1})$ and $P_{2}$ have the same number of roots (previous proposition) and that roots of an irreducible polynomial has the same multiplicity, we have by the previous proposition that :

$\sigma^{X}_{f}(P_{1})(X)=\prod_{k=1}^{m}(X-Q_{f}(\alpha_{k}))^{r}\quad\text{and}\quad P_{2}(X)=\prod_{k=1}^{m}(X-\alpha_{k})^{r}$

Where $\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{m}$ are the distinct roots of $P_{2}$ and $r$ is the degree of $P_{2}$ over $m$. Hence, we have :

$(\sigma^{X}_{f}(P_{1})\circ Q)(X)=\prod_{k=1}^{m}(Q(X)-Q_{f}(\alpha_{k}))^{r}.$

The $Q_{f}(\alpha_{k})$’s are distinct (previous proposition). Hence, the multplicity of $\alpha_{k}$ as a root $\sigma^{X}_{f}(P_{1})\circ Q$ is equal to the multiplicity of $\alpha_{k}$ for the factor $(Q(X)-Q_{f}(\alpha_{k}))^{r}$. By proposition 2.4 $\sigma^{X}_{f}(P_{1})\circ Q=S_{f}P_{2}$; we have seen that $P_{2}(X)=\prod_{k=1}^{m}(X-\alpha_{k})^{r}$ and $P_{2}$ is irreducible. Hence, $S_{f}$ is prime to $P_{2}$ if and only $f$ the multiplicity of $\alpha_{k}$ for the factor $(Q(X)-Q_{f}(\alpha_{k}))^{r}$ is $r$. This last condition is equivalent to $Q^{\prime}(\alpha_{k})\neq 0$. Since $P_{2}$ is irreducible and $\alpha_{k}$ is a root of $P_{2}$ and degree of $Q_{f}$ is less than the degree of $P_{2}$, the condition $Q^{\prime}(\alpha_{k})\neq 0$ is equivalent to the condition $Q^{\prime}\neq 0$. We have proved that $S_{f}$ is prime to $P_{2}$ if and only if $Q^{\prime}\neq 0$. ∎

label: Theorem 2.8
content: $\Bbbk$ is a field and $P_{1},P_{2}$ are irreducible polynomials in $\Bbbk[X]$. Take $n>1$. If $f:\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1})\to\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2})$ is a ring isomorphism stabilising $\Bbbk$, then $f_{X,n}:\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1}^{n})\to\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2}^{n})$ of Proposition 2.4 is a ring isomorphism stabilising $\Bbbk$ if and only if $Q^{\prime}_{f}\neq 0$.
proof: This is obtained by combining the last proposition with proposition 2.5 ∎

label: Corollary 2.9
content: $\Bbbk$ is a field and $P_{1},P_{2}$ are irreducible polynomials in $\Bbbk[X]$. If $f:\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1})\to\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2})$ is a ring isomorphism stabilising $\Bbbk$ such that $Q^{\prime}_{f}\neq 0$, then $\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1}^{n})\to\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2}^{n})$ are isomorphic for al $n\geq 1$.

label: Theorem 2.10
content: $\Bbbk$ is a field and $P_{1},P_{2}$ are irreducible polynomials in $\Bbbk[X]$. Let $f_{m}:\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1}^{m})\to\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2}^{m})$ be a ring isomorphism stabilizing $\Bbbk$ for a given $m\geq 1$.The map $f_{m}$ maps the class of $X$ onto the class of some $R\in\Bbbk[X]$. Let $Q$ be the reminder of the division of $R$ by $P_{2}$ ($Q$ does not depend on the choice of $R$). If $Q^{\prime}\neq 0$, then the rings $\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1}^{n})$ and $\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2}^{n})$ are isomorphic for all $n\geq 1$.
proof: Since $\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1}^{m})$ and $\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1}^{m})$ have a unique maximal ideal, $f_{m}$ induces a ring isomorphism stabilising $\Bbbk$ $f:\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1})\to\Bbbk[X]/(P_{2})$ of the residue fields. Now $Q_{f}=Q$ and hence $Q^{\prime}_{f}\neq 0$ and by the previous theorem the morphisms $f_{X,n}:\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1})\to\Bbbk[X]/(P_{1}^{n})$ are isomorphisms.
